titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — Epilogue IV: the last curses (xliii 81 – xliv 91)
part: Epilogue IV · the last curses (Col. xliii 81 – xliv 91)
about: The fourth and last part of the epilogue finishes the curses on a later king who destroys or alters the stele, and with it the stele and the code. Zamama, the warrior at the king’s right hand, is asked to break the wrongdoer’s weapon in battle, turn his day into night and set his enemy over him (xliii 81–91). Ištar, lady of battle, is asked, in her anger, to curse his kingship, to turn his good into evil, to set confusion and revolt on him, to make his warriors fall and the earth drink their blood, to heap his army’s corpses in the open country and to give him bound into his enemy’s hand (xliii 92 – xliv 23). Nergal, the strong one among the gods, is asked to burn his people like a fire in a reed-bed, to bring him to an end with his strong weapon (?) and to smash his body like a clay figure (xliv 24–39). Nintu is asked to take a son and a name from him and to let him beget no seed (xliv 40–49). Ninkarrak, the daughter of Anum, is asked to send a heavy sickness on him that no physician can cure, until his life is destroyed (xliv 50–69). Last, the great gods of heaven and earth and the Anunnaki are asked to curse him, his seed, his land, his army and his people, and Ellil, with the word that is never changed, to curse him and let the curse overtake him quickly (xliv 70–91). This is the end of the text on the stele. The stele is read through Harper’s 1904 transliteration and his plates; a number of words in these curses are rare, the readings are his or mine, and the notes say where they are uncertain.

sentences.l: Zamama, the-warrior the-great, the-son the-first of-Ekur, going at-my-right,
sentences.i: Zamama, the great warrior, the first son (?) of Ekur, who goes at my right hand,
sentences.n: A new god, and a new paragraph of curses. {d}za-ma₃-ma₃ is Zamama: the god’s name spelled with the signs ZA, MA₃, MA₃, as at xl 22 (Harper prints ZA.MA(L).MA(L), and his sign list shows the same group), after the silent divine determinative AN. qarrādum rabûm is “the great warrior”, two nominatives in -um; the first sign is GAR, read qar (Harper prints it gar here and qar at xliv 8). mār rēštûm: Harper prints mar+ri-eš-tu-um as one word, with a plus where the plate shows a cross-like mark; I read mar “son” and rēštûm “first, foremost” (the adjective of the glossary), so “the first son”. That this means “first-born son” is UNCERTAIN, and so is the division into two words. ša Ekur is “of Ekur”, Enlil’s temple (É.KUR, as at xlii 81). ālik imnīya “who goes at my right”: ālik is the participle of alākum, written a-li-ku with the -u kept before the genitive (as mušarriku at xlii 101), and imnīya is imittum “right side” + -ia, “my right”: the god who walks beside the king as his helper. The wishes follow in the next two units.

sentences.l: in-the-place of-battle his-weapon let-him-break,
sentences.i: in the place of battle may he break his weapon,
sentences.n: ašar tamḫārim “in the place of battle”: ašar is ašrum “place” in the construct, and tamḫārim is “of battle” (tamḫārum, spelled tam-ḫa-ri-im with the UD sign read tam). kakkašu “his weapon”: GIŠ.TUKUL is the Sumerogram for kakkum with no ending written (as kakkim at xl 22), then the sign ŠU “his”; the second sign is keyed TUK, as in epilogue-1 (TENTATIVE). lišbir “let him break” is the precative of šebērum “to break” (the glossary has the preterite išbir). The subject is still Zamama; as in the other curses, a wish for the ruin of the king who destroys the stele.

sentences.l: day into-night let-him-turn-for-him-and, his-enemy against-him let-him-set-up.
sentences.i: may he turn the day into night for him, and set his enemy up against him.
sentences.n: ūmam “the day” (accusative): UD with the ending written out, -ma-am; Harper’s û is the UD sign, as in epilogue-3 at xliii 1. ana mūšim “into night” (mūšum “night”, mu-ši-im). litēršumma is the D precative of târum + -šum “for him” + -ma “and”: with ana “into” it means “turn (day) into night for him”. At xliii 1 and 45 (epilogue-3) the same verb has -šu “from him” and was rendered “turn away from him” (UNCERTAIN there as here). nakiršu elīšu lišziz “let him set his enemy up against him”: nakiršu is nakrum “enemy” + -šu, elīšu is eli “over, against” + -šu, and lišziz is the Š precative of izuzzum “to stand”, “let him make (his enemy) stand”. The curse of Zamama ends with this unit.

sentences.l: Ištar, lady of-battle and of-combats, the-opener of-my-weapons,
sentences.i: Ištar, lady of battle and fighting, who opens my weapons (?),
sentences.n: A new goddess. {d}INANNA is Ištar (Harper normalises Nanâ); the same sign as at xl 22. bēlit “lady of” (be-li-it, the construct of bēltum). taḫāzim “of battle”: on the plate this is one broad sign group (a vertical with a long horizontal bar and a stack of small wedges, with no ending), which is the AK sign (Harper’s sign list no. 48, ag, ak: the same sign as in ag-gi-im at xliii 100), not the ME sign (no. 184, a vertical with a bar). I do not know which Sumerogram it is: Harper gives only the normalized word (his glossary TAḪAZU “battle, conflict”, xliii 93 and xliv 2, beside KABLU “battle” for the next sign), so the word is read from his normalization and its sense is UNCERTAIN; the key AK is the sign’s shape only. ù “and” (U3). qablê “of combats”: two identical signs, which I read as MURUB₄ twice (Harper’s sign list no. 6, qablu); a doubled sign is a plural, as in ilī (NI.NI). The key MURUB4 is new here and its Unicode stand-in (SHU2) does not look like the plate’s box sign, so the key is TENTATIVE; the identification rests on Harper’s no. 6, which the plate group matches. pātiat kakkīya “who opens my weapons”: pātiat is the feminine participle of petûm “to open” (pa-ti-a-at), kakkīya is kakkum + -ia, GIŠ.TUKUL again. That a goddess “opens” the king’s weapons (sets them free for use) is my reading of the grammar; the picture is UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: my-lamassu gracious, the-lover of-my-reign,
sentences.i: my gracious guardian spirit, who loves my reign,
sentences.n: lamassī damiqtum “my gracious guardian spirit”: lamassum is the protective spirit of the glossary; la-ma-zi is lamassī “my lamassu”, the zi standing for -ssī (at xl 53 the -ia is written out), and damiqtum is the feminine of damqum “good, gracious” (the IG sign read iq; Harper prints it with a dotted q). rāʾimat palêya “who loves my reign”: rāʾimat is the feminine participle of râmum “to love” in the construct (ra-i-ma-at), and palêya is BALA + -ia, “my reign”, as at xlii 45. The unit has no verb; the goddess is still being named, and the curses begin at 99.

sentences.l: in her-heart enraged, in her-wrath great, his-kingship let-her-curse,
sentences.i: In her angry heart, in her great wrath, may she curse his kingship,
sentences.n: ina libbiša aggim “in her heart, enraged”: libbiša is libbum + -ša “her”, and aggim is the genitive of aggum “angry”, agreeing with it (ag-gi-im, the AK sign read ag; Harper’s glossary has AGGU “anger”, a noun, and the adjective “angry” is my reading, UNCERTAIN; the word is not in the earlier glossaries). ina uzzatiša rabêtim “in her wrath, great”: uzzatum “wrath, anger” + -ša (uz-za-ti-ša), with rabêtim, the feminine plural genitive of rabûm; uz-za-ti-ša itself is a singular form, so the plural adjective makes the noun a plural of intensity, “her great fury”, UNCERTAIN (Harper’s glossary has UZZATU “fury”). šarrūssu lirur “let her curse his kingship”: šarrūssu is šarrūtum + -šu, the zu spelling -ssu as in mātassu, and lirur is the precative of arārum, as in epilogue-1 to -3. The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.l: his-good-things into-evil let-her-turn.
sentences.i: may she turn his good things into evil.
sentences.n: damqātišu “his good things”: the plural of damqum “good” in the feminine (dam-qa₂-ti-šu, the GA sign read qa₂; Harper prints ga), with -šu “his”; ana lemnētim “into evil” (lemnum, spelled li-im-ne-tim as in the glossary, a feminine plural, “evil things”). litēr is the D precative of târum, “let her turn”, with ana “into” exactly as at xliii 79 (epilogue-3). The column ends on li-te-ir (xliii 106); the next column begins with li-te-ir again (see the next unit).

sentences.l: (let-her-turn); in-the-place of-battle and of-combats his-weapon let-her-break,
sentences.i: (may she turn — the verb repeated;) in the place of battle and fighting may she break his weapon,
sentences.n: XLIV 1 repeats li-te-ir “let her turn”: the plate shows the verb at the foot of the last column and again at the head of this one, as Harper prints it. I take the second as a scribe’s repetition at the top of a new column and not a new wish, because the sense runs straight from “into evil let her turn” (xliii 104–106) to “in the place of battle …”; that is UNCERTAIN. ašar taḫāzim u qablê “in the place of battle and of combats” is as at xliii 93, with the same two TENTATIVE signs (AK for taḫāzim, MURUB₄ twice for qablê); line 2 is a tall ruled line on the plate with a second tier (Harper’s {b}) for u qablê, so it is one stele line. kakkašu lišbir “let her break his weapon”, as xliii 87; the goddess is now the subject, since the curse of Ištar goes on.

sentences.l: confusion, revolt let-her-set for-him,
sentences.i: may she set confusion (?) and revolt (?) upon him,
sentences.n: i-ši-tam and za-aḫ-ma-aš-tam are two feminine accusatives, objects of liškunšum, “let her set (them) for him” (the G precative of šakānum, as at xliii 30 in epilogue-3, li-iš-ku-un-šum). Harper’s glossary has both nouns: IŠÎTU “confusion, revolt” and SAḪMAŠTU “revolt”, which he files under S (so the normalized word is saḫmaštam; the ZA sign is read sa there, as in his zi-im-di for simdu). I take “confusion” and “revolt” from him, UNCERTAIN, since neither word can be checked from the grammar. They fit a list of misfortunes set on the king.

sentences.l: his-warriors let-her-make-fall, their-blood the-earth let-her-give-to-drink.
sentences.i: may she make his warriors fall, and make the earth drink their blood.
sentences.n: qarrādīšu “his warriors” (qarrādum + -šu, GAR read qar; Harper prints it with a dotted q). lišamqit “let her make fall”: the Š precative of maqātum “to fall” (li-ša-am-qi₂-it, the KI sign read qi₂; Harper prints ki). dāmīšunu is “their blood” (damum, plural dāmū, + -šunu). erṣetam lišqi “let her give the earth to drink”: erṣetam is the accusative of erṣetum “earth” (ir-ṣi-tam), and lišqi is the precative of šaqûm “to give to drink” (li-iš-qi₂, KI again; Harper prints ki); šaqûm takes two accusatives, “make the earth drink their blood”. The reading of KI as qi₂ in both verbs rests on the roots maqātum and šaqûm.

sentences.l: a-heap of-the-corpses of-his-troops in-the-open-country let-her-cast.
sentences.i: may she cast down a heap of the corpses of his troops in the open country.
sentences.n: gurun šalmat ummānātišu: gurun is the construct of gurunnum “heap, pile” (Harper’s GURUNNU, at this line; it is not in the earlier glossaries), šalmat is the construct of šalmatum “corpse”, and ummānātišu is “of his troops” (ummānum “army, host”, with the plural -āt, + -šu). ina ṣērim “in the open country” (the glossary’s ṣērum). littaddi is the precative of nadûm “to throw, cast”, in a stem with infixed -t- (li-it-ta-ad-di); Harper files it under nadû I,2 (the stem with infixed -t-), so the exact stem is UNCERTAIN, the sense “cast down” is not.

sentences.l: his-army […]-am, may-she-not let-obtain him.
sentences.i: His army … (a stretch of about five signs is broken away) …; may she not let him obtain …
sentences.n: A gap. Line 17 begins with ṣābašu “his army” (ERIN₂, Harper’s sign list no. 152, ṣābu, with -šu) and then the plate shows hatched, broken stone, which Harper prints as five dots, and only the last sign, am, is clear; before it the plate shows traces of more than one further sign, one half under the hatching and one fairly clear (a box with three ticks), that Harper does not transliterate and I cannot identify. The stretch is shown as a gap and nothing is restored. The next line ay ušarši šuāti “may she not let him obtain” (ay + the preterite of the Š stem of rašûm, as ay ušabši in epilogue-3; šuāti is the accusative “him”) needs an object that is lost in the damage, so the sentence cannot be read through. The loss is on the stele itself, not in this edition.

sentences.l: into-the-hand of-his-enemy let-her-deliver-him-and, to-the-land of-his-hostility bound let-them-drive-him.
sentences.i: may she hand him over into the hand of his enemy, and may they lead him bound to his enemy’s land.
sentences.n: ana qāt nakrišu “into the hand of his enemy” (qāt, spelled qa₂-at; Harper prints ga-at; nakrum + -šu). limallišuma is the D precative of malûm “to fill” + -šu “him” + -ma “and”; the D stem, with ana qāt, is the idiom “to hand over to”. ana māt nukurtišu “to the land of his hostility”, that is, his enemy’s land (as ina māt nukurtim in the glossary; nukurtum “enmity”). kamiš lirʾûšu: kamiš is an adverb in -iš, “bound, in bonds” (from kamûm “to bind”), and lirʾûšu is “let them herd him”, the precative of rêʾûm “to pasture, herd” in the 3rd plural + -šu (li-ru-šu, the ru spelling ruʾ). Both words are UNCERTAIN: Harper’s glossary files li-ru-šu (with li-ri, as in epilogue-2) under ARU II,1 “to carry, to rule”, and has KAMÎŠ “bound” as its own entry; I keep the house reading of that verb as rêʾûm (epilogue-2, “shepherd, rule”) and render “lead”, the shepherd’s verb for a captive. Lines 20 and 22 have second tiers on the plate (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.l: Nergal, the-strong among-the-gods, of-battle none-to-face, who-brings-about my-victory,
sentences.i: Nergal, the strong one among the gods, whose battle none can face, who brings about my victory,
sentences.n: A new god. {d}NER.URU.GAL is Nergal, written with the signs NER (keyed KIŠ), URU and GAL, as in Harper’s sign list no. 170. dannum ina ilī “the strong one among the gods” (ilī is the doubled sign NI.NI, as at xlii 22). qabal lā maḫār “battle none can face”: qabal is the construct of qablum “battle” (qa₂-ba-al; Harper prints ga-ba-al) and lā maḫār the infinitive of maḫārum “to face” with the negative (ma-ḫa-ar); the glossary has the same phrase in the genitive, qabal lā maḫārim; line 26 has a second tier on the plate (Harper’s {b}). mušakšidu irnittīya “who brings about my victory”: mušakšidu is the Š participle of kašādum “to reach” (“who makes (me) reach”), with the -u kept, as mušarriku at xlii 101; irnittīya is irnittum “victory” + -ia (the form irnitti before a genitive, then -ia).

sentences.l: by-his-great kašūšu, like-a-fire fierce of-the-reed-thicket, his-people let-him-burn,
sentences.i: by his great might (?), like the fierce fire of a reed thicket may he burn up his people,
sentences.n: ina kašūšišu rabîm “by his great kašūšu”: kašūšum is Harper’s word (ka-šu-ši-šu is kašūšišu); Harper’s glossary has KAŠÛŠU “power, strength”, which I take, and the sense is UNCERTAIN (a word for a divine weapon is also possible). kīma išātim izzitim ša apim “like a fierce fire of the reed thicket”: išātim and izzitim are genitives (ezzum “fierce”, with i for e, as at xliii 76), and ša a-bi-im is “of the reed thicket” (apum “reed-bed, thicket”, the BI sign read pi₂ or bi; Harper’s glossary has ABU “cane, reeds” at this line, which I follow, and a-bi-im could also be abim “of the father”, which does not fit the picture). nišīšu liqme “let him burn his people”: nišīšu is nišū “people” + -šu; liqme is the precative of qamûm “to burn” (li-iq-me, the IG sign read iq; Harper prints li-ik-me), UNCERTAIN as a form; the sense is Harper’s (his glossary has KAMU I,1 “to burn”, li-ik-me, at this line). Line 32 has a second tier on the plate (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.l: with-his-weapon strong let-him-bring-to-an-end him-and, his-body like-an-image of-clay let-him-smash.
sentences.i: with his strong weapon let him bring him to an end (?), and smash his body like a clay figure.
sentences.n: ina kakkišu dannim “with his strong weapon”: in is the IN sign for ina (the plate has no a here; Harper prints in), kakkišu is GIŠ.TUKUL + -šu, and dannim is dannum in the genitive (the word is broken between the pages of Harper’s print, XLIV 35 dan- and nim). li-ša-ti-šu-ma is, I take it, lišaqtišuma: Harper’s glossary files this form under KATÛ III,1 “to bring to an end, to cut off” as li-ša-[ak]-ti-šu (the aq bracketed, so not in his transliteration; it is the same Š precative as lišaqti at xliii 56 in epilogue-3), with -šu “him” and -ma “and”. I could not tell on the plate whether a further sign stands between ša and ti, so the spelling and the reading are UNCERTAIN; the glyphs below are Harper’s transliteration’s. biniātišu “his body”: Harper’s BINÛTU “muscle, life” (biniātu, plural, + -šu); “body” is my choice, UNCERTAIN. kīma ṣalam ṭīṭim “like an image of clay” (ṣalmum “statue”, ṭīṭum “clay”; the plate has two DI signs, ṭi-ṭi-im; Harper prints di-di-im). liḫpuš “let him smash”: the G precative of ḫapāšum “to break, to crush, to shatter” (Harper’s ḪAPAŠU I,1, li-iḫ-pu-uš, at this line); “smash” is his sense.

sentences.l: Nintu, lady exalted of-the-lands, the-mother my-creator,
sentences.i: Nintu, the exalted lady of the lands, the mother, my creator,
sentences.n: A new goddess. {d}NIN.TU is Nintu “lady of birth” (the signs NIN and TU after the silent determinative). bēltum ṣīrtum “the exalted lady”: NIN is bēltum (as at xlii 81) and ṣi-ir-tum is the feminine of ṣīrum “lofty, exalted”. ša mātātim “of the lands” (mātātim, the plural of mātum, ma-ta-tim). ummum bānītī “the mother, my creator”: ummum is the sign AMA (as at xlii 81–82), bānītī is the feminine participle of banûm “to create” + -ī “my” (ba-ni-ti), “my creator” (feminine; Harper’s BANÎTU “mother”), as bānî “my creator” (masculine) at xliii 41 (epilogue-3).

sentences.l: a-son let-her-turn-away-from-him-and, a-name may-she-not let-him-obtain, in-the-midst of-his-people the-seed of-mankind may-he-not beget.
sentences.i: May she turn a son away from him, and may she not let him obtain a name; may he not beget the seed of mankind among his people.
sentences.n: māram litēršuma “let her turn a son away from him, and”: māram is DUMU (the sign TUR) with the ending -am (Harper prints mâram), and litēršuma is the verb of xliii 1 and 45 (epilogue-3), “let her turn (it) away from him”, UNCERTAIN as there. Line 44 is two ruled rows on the plate with Harper’s {b}, one stele line. šumam “a name” (šumum). ay ušaršīšu “may she not let him obtain”: ay with the preterite, as in epilogue-3, of the Š stem of rašûm “to get” + -šu “him” (u-šar-ši-šu); a name is the first thing he is to be denied, after a son. ina kirbit nišīšu “in the midst of his people” (kirbit is Harper’s kirbitu “midst”, kir-bi-it, UNCERTAIN as a word; nišīšu, nišū + -šu). zēr awīlūtim “the seed of mankind”: zēr is the sign ZIR (Harper’s zêr) and awīlūtim the genitive of awīlūtum; ay ibni “may he not create (beget)”, ay with the preterite of banûm. Lines 44, 46 and 47 have second tiers on the plate (Harper’s {b}). The curse is that the wrongdoer have no offspring.

sentences.l: Ninkarrak, daughter of-Anum, who-speaks my-favour in-Ekur,
sentences.i: Ninkarrak, the daughter of Anum, who speaks of my kindness (?) in Ekur,
sentences.n: A new goddess. {d}NIN.KAR.RA.AK is Ninkarrak, written with the signs NIN, KAR, RA, AK (Harper’s name); the physician-goddess. mārat Anim “daughter of Anum”: mārat is DUMU with the ending written -at (the glossary’s mārtum), and AN.NIM is Anim, the genitive of Anum, the two signs AN and NIM. qābiat dumqīya “who speaks my favor”: qābiat is the feminine participle of qabûm “to speak” (qa₂-bi-a-at; Harper prints ga-bi-a-at), and dumqīya is dumqum “kindness, favor” + -ia (dum-qi₂-ia, KI read qi₂; Harper prints dum-ki-ia): “who speaks of my kindness”, UNCERTAIN as an idiom (Harper’s DUMKU is “favor”). ina Ekur “in Ekur” (É.KUR; Harper prints Ê with a circumflex here and plain E elsewhere). The curses follow in the next units.

sentences.l: an-illness heavy, an-ašakku evil, a-wound painful,
sentences.i: a heavy illness, an evil ašakku, a painful wound,
sentences.n: Three accusatives, objects of lišaṣiaššumma at xliv 65. murṣam kabtam “a heavy illness” (murṣum “illness”, the HAR sign read mur; kab-tam, kabtum “heavy, severe”). ašakkam lemnam “an evil ašakku”: ašakku is the name of a sickness (a sickness-demon), written on the plate with two signs, Á (A₂) and a second sign that I do not identify; Harper’s sign list no. 129 gives the two signs together as ašakku (his glossary: ASAKKU “disease”) and draws the second as a vertical wedge with a box of bars, as on the plate; I cannot identify it. The key LAL (his no. 181, a plain hooked vertical) is only a placeholder and is not the plate’s shape, so the second sign is shown as ?; UNCERTAIN. ṣimmam marṣam “a painful wound”: ṣimmum “wound” (the sign ZI read ṣi, as in the glossary’s ṣimmam kabtam; Harper prints zi-im-ma-am), with marṣam “sick, painful”. Lines 55 and 57 each have a second tier on the plate (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.l: which the-physician does-not-calm, its-inside he-does-not-know,
sentences.i: which the physician cannot soothe, whose inside he does not understand,
sentences.n: A relative clause on the three sicknesses: ša lā ipaššeḫu asûm “which the physician does not calm” (ipaššeḫu, the present of pašāḫum “to become calm, to calm”, with the -u of a ša-clause; pašāḫum is not in the earlier glossaries; Harper’s PAŠAḪU I,1 is “to be healed, to be cured”, which would make the verb intransitive, “which does not get well”, with the physician then the subject of the next clause only: UNCERTAIN), and kirībšu lā ilammadu “its inside he does not know” (kirbum “inside” + -šu; ilammadu, the present of lamādum “to know” with the -u of the clause). asûm “the physician” is A.ZU, the two signs A and ZU (Harper’s ȧ-su; the dot he prints over the a is no sign), with no ending written, as in the glossary’s asâm; he is the subject of both clauses, and the pair of verbs says that no physician’s skill reaches the sickness.

sentences.l: with-a-bandage he-does-not-give-him-ease, like-the-bite of-death which-is-not removed,
sentences.i: with a bandage he cannot give him ease, like the bite of death that cannot be removed,
sentences.n: ina ṣimdi lā unaḫḫuššu: ṣimdi is “by a bandage” (written zi-im-di; Harper’s SIMDU “bandage”, which I follow, with ZI read ṣi as in ṣimmum), and lā unaḫḫuššu is unaḫḫuš, the D present of naḫûm “to be quiet” (Harper’s NAḪU II,1 “to pacify, to allay”; D, “to give ease to”), + -šu “him”, the š of the stem and the š of -šu written once (u-na-aḫ-ḫu-šu, split over two tiers on the plate); the subject is the physician of the last unit. kīma nišiq mūtim lā innassaḫu “like the bite of death that is not removed”: nišiq is the construct of nišqum (Harper’s NIŠQU “bite”, written ni-ši-iq with the IG sign read iq), so “the bite of death”; it is not našāqum “to kiss”, and the exact sense is UNCERTAIN. mūtim is “of death” (mūtum, with long ū; mutum “husband” is a different word), and innassaḫu is the N present of nasāḫum “to pull out, remove” with the -u of the clause (in-na-za-ḫu, with za for -ssa- as in the glossary’s innassaḫ): the sickness cannot be pulled out of him.

sentences.l: in his-body let-her-bring-out-for-him-and, until his-life they-destroy,
sentences.i: and may she make them break out on him in his body, until they destroy his life,
sentences.n: ina biniātišu “in his body” (as at xliv 37; UNCERTAIN as a word). lišaṣiaššumma “let her bring (them) out for him, and”: the Š precative of waṣûm “to go out” (li-ša-ṣi-…), with the ventive -am and the dative -šum fused (aš-šum) and -ma; “bring out” here means make the sicknesses break out on him. The object is the three sicknesses of xliv 55–57. adi napištašu ibêllû “until they put out his life”: adi “until”, napištašu is napištum “life” + -šu (na-bi-iš-ta-šu, b for p), ibêllû the present, 3rd plural, of balûm (Harper’s BALÛ I,1 “to destroy”, which lists this very form; his II,1 “to extinguish” is the D stem) with the -u of the clause; the subject is the sicknesses, and the sense “destroy” is Harper’s, UNCERTAIN as to the exact verb. Lines 64–66 have second tiers on the plate (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.l: for his-manhood let-him-mourn.
sentences.i: may he mourn for his manhood (?).
sentences.n: ana idlūtišu “for his manhood”: idlūtum “manhood, vigor” (Harper’s glossary has EDLUTU “manhood, vigor”, ed-lu-ti-šu, at this line; the plate sign A₂ is read id here, so id-lu-ti-šu) + -šu. liddammam “let him mourn” is Harper’s DAMAMU I,2 “to lament” (a t-stem, li-id-dam-ma-am, with the ventive -am); the exact form, and the reading of idlūtum as “manhood”, are UNCERTAIN, and “mourn for his manhood” is the sense that suits the curse (the sickness unmans him before it kills him). This closes the curse of Ninkarrak.

sentences.l: the-gods the-great of-heaven and of-earth, the-Anunnaki, in their-assembly,
sentences.i: May the great gods of heaven and earth, the Anunnaki, in their assembly
sentences.n: The next paragraph calls the great gods as a body. ilâni rabûti “the great gods”: DINGIR (the AN sign alone) and GAL.GAL, as at xl 40 (epilogue-1). ša šamê u erṣetim “of heaven and earth” (ša-me-e, ir-ṣi-tim). {d}A.NUN.NA is the Anunnaki, the gods as a college (the prologue spells it out syllabically). ina puḫrišunu “in their assembly”: puḫrum “assembly” + -šunu; the plate writes puḫri as a compound sign (ŠU with a box sign, as in Harper’s sign list no. 138, puḫru, in modern notation ŠU.NIGIN); I key it ŠU.LAGAB, and the second sign is TENTATIVE. The verb of the sentence is lirurū at xliv 83, and it has several objects before it.

sentences.l: wall(?) of-the-house, the-brickwork of-Ebabbar, him, his-seed, his-land, his-army, his-people and his-troops,
sentences.i: the wall (?) of the house, the brickwork of Ebabbar, him, his seed, his land, his army, his people and his troops,
sentences.n: A list of objects, with a first stretch that I cannot construe; I give the words and say what is unclear. še-it bi-tim: Harper’s šêt bîtim; šēt is his ŠĒTU “wall (?)” (his query), so “the wall (?) of the house”, UNCERTAIN, and bītim is “of the house”. libit Ebabbara “the brickwork of Ebabbar”: SIG₄ is libittum (as libit Esagila at xli 48, TENTATIVE sign) and É.BABBAR.RA is Ebabbar, Šamaš’s temple (the glossary’s Ebabbar, with the ending RA). šuāti is the accusative of šū, which Harper glosses “that” (demonstrative, here and at xliv 19): “that (one)” or “him”; I do not know whether it points to the wrongdoer, to the brickwork or to the whole phrase, so I render “him” as at xliv 19 and leave it open. zēršu mātassu ṣābašu nišīšu u ummānšu “his seed, his land, his army, his people and his troops”: five objects (ZIR + -šu; mātassu as before; ERIN₂ + -šu, Harper’s sign list no. 152; nišū + -šu; ummānum + -šu, written syllabically); their verb is lirurū at xliv 83.

sentences.l: a-curse grievous let-them-curse,
sentences.i: curse (him) with a grievous curse,
sentences.n: irritam marūštam lirurū “let them curse with a grievous curse”: irritam is the accusative of irritum “curse” (Harper’s IRRITU; ir-ri-tam), marūštam “grievous” (as in epilogue-3), and lirurū is the precative of arārum with the plural -ū (li-ru-ru), the verb for all the objects of the last unit; the “curse” is the cognate object, “let them curse him a curse”.

sentences.l: with-curses mighty
sentences.i: with mighty curses,
sentences.n: irrītim danniātim “with mighty curses”: the genitive, here taken as a plural, of irritum (ir-ri-tim) and the feminine plural genitive of dannum (da-ni-a-tim); there is no ina, the genitive stands as an instrument. These two words may belong to the verb that ends the sentence, liruršuma at xliv 89, rather than to lirurū; the sense is the same either way, and I leave them between the two sentences.

sentences.l: Ellil, with-his-mouth which not is-changed, let-him-curse-him-and,
sentences.i: Ellil, with his mouth that is never changed, may he curse him, and
sentences.n: A last god. {d}EN.LÍL is Ellil, the name of xl 11 and xlii 53 (epilogue-1 and -2): the divine determinative, EN and the sign KID (LÍL). Harper normalizes the group Bêl, and his sign list (no. 49, the line “Bêl”) draws EN with a following box sign, as on the plate. ina pîšu “with his mouth” (the sign KA, pûm, + -šu). ša lā uttakkaru “which is not changed”: ša, lā and the D-t present of nakārum with the -u of the clause (ut-ta-ak-ka-ru, the UD sign read ut), the same verb as uttakkaru at xlii 53 (epilogue-2): his spoken word is never altered. liruršuma “let him curse him, and”: the precative lirur of arārum + -šu “him” + -ma “and” (li-ru-ur-šu-ma; no long vowel is written, so it is short, as in lirur). Line 88 has a second tier on the plate (Harper’s {b} inside ut-ta-ak-ka-ru).

sentences.l: quickly let-it-overtake-him.
sentences.i: and may the curse overtake him quickly.
sentences.n: arḫiš “quickly” (the adverb of the glossary). likšudaššu “let it overtake him”: the precative of kašādum “to reach, overtake” with the ventive -am and -šu fused (li-ik-šu-da-šu; the IG sign read ik); the subject is Ellil’s curse. The text of the stele ends with this word; Harper’s last plate has nothing after it.
